stage_description: The mature adult is middle-aged, from about 3 years until the senior stage begins — an onset that depends on size: giant breeds reach it by 5–6 years, small breeds after 10–11. The dog is still in its prime, but this is exactly when early detection of chronic disease and weight control matter most to extend active, healthy years.
nutrition: A maintenance adult diet with calorie control, since a slowing metabolism raises the risk of weight gain. If the dog tends to gain weight, adjust portions or switch to a lower-calorie food on veterinary advice, and weigh regularly.
activity: Keep up regular physical and mental activity matched to individual stamina. Maintaining muscle tone and a healthy weight helps protect the joints and heart through the coming senior years.
veterinary_check_frequency: An exam once a year; for large and giant breeds, consider visits every 6 months with baseline bloodwork to catch age-related changes before symptoms appear.
dental_care: Regular home toothbrushing and an annual professional oral assessment; periodontal disease becomes more common with age and can affect the heart and kidneys.
warning_signs: Gradual weight change, increased thirst and urination, new lumps or bumps under the skin, reduced stamina, or bad breath. These signs warrant a veterinary evaluation.
disclaimer: This information is for educational purposes only and does not replace consultation with a veterinarian.
